column4: The disciples want to eat from the heavenly table and have their hearts reassured; the meal is expected to answer both bodily and inward lack, exactly the two-function test applied to food in the section.
Jesus asks for the table as a feast, a sign, and provision and calls God the best Provider; this is food whose abundance of functions directly reverses the uselessness of ضَرِيع.
The disciples ask whether a table can be sent from heaven; this ayah stages the requested food-object whose purposes 5:113-114 then make explicit.
God grants the table but attaches an unparalleled punishment to disbelief afterward, marking bestowed food as both provision and a test rather than an automatic guarantee of safety.
A visitation from the Lord strikes the owners' food garden while they sleep, beginning a scene in which expected produce is withheld.
The garden becomes like a stripped or harvested field; productive vegetation has become empty plant-remnant, close to the section's dried thorn image.
The owners resolve that no poor person will enter the garden, making deliberate denial of food to the needy part of the scene that ends in their own deprivation.
On recognizing the ruined garden they say that they are deprived; the word “deprived” states the same unremoved lack reached after the crop is lost.

A fruit garden is struck by a fiery whirlwind precisely when its aged owner and weak offspring need it; provision turns to ash at the point of greatest dependence, a sharp indirect parallel to food that cannot answer need.
After listing forbidden foods, the ayah permits necessity under severe hunger; the legal boundary itself recognizes that hunger is a bodily lack food must answer.
Feeding ten poor people is measured by the average food one gives one's own family, supplying a concrete Quranic standard for food adequate enough to count as feeding.
Livestock provide warmth, benefits, and food; they realize the bodily abundance suggested by the section's “large-uddered ewe” sense instead of leaving it unheard and unused.
God makes livestock for riding and eating, another direct herd-as-provision scene opposite the dry plant that cannot nourish.
Livestock are made for carrying loads and for food, and people are told to eat God's provision; the animal and Provider details meet the section's ewe and nourishment images.
Sacrificial camels become food both for the worshippers and for the contented and asking poor, joining livestock nourishment to the duty of relieving another's need.
Pilgrims are told to eat from sacrificial animals and feed the miserable poor, a concrete distribution of nourishing food against the scene of need left intact.
Dates and grapes yield both intoxicant and good provision; the ayah distinguishes products made from fruitful plants and identifies a genuinely good provision, unlike the single dried thorn.
The bee's varied drink contains healing for people; a consumed liquid that benefits the body is the functional reverse of the section's thin-drink echo and Hell's injurious drinks.
The question asks who could bring flowing water if people's water sank away; it makes the availability of relieving drink depend upon the Provider.
Water descends in due measure and is lodged in the earth, while God can remove it; drinkable provision is both fitted to need and explicitly contingent.
God sends water from the sky and gives it to people to drink while they cannot store its source, clarifying who supplies the drink-side of bodily need.
Pure water descends before the drinking scene of 25:49, the opposite in quality and effect to boiling or foul liquids offered in punishment.
The water revives dead land and gives drink to livestock and many people, uniting living vegetation, herds, and effective relief of thirst.
The promised Garden has food that endures and shade that endures; lasting food and functioning shade jointly reverse both ضَرِيع and the shade that does not avail in 77:31.
The good tree gives its fruit continually by its Lord's permission, a productive plant defined by repeated nourishment rather than dryness and failure.
The bad word is like a tree uprooted from the earth with no stability; it supplies the barren tree-side boundary to the fruitful tree in 14:25, though it is not itself presented as food.
Garden shade is brought close and fruit clusters are lowered within reach, pairing effective shelter with accessible food against the false shade and false meal of punishment.
Their Lord gives them a pure drink, a direct positive reversal of punitive drink and of the thin-drink sense heard beside ضَرِيع.
Golden platters and cups circulate with everything souls desire, presenting serving vessels and desired intake where Hell offers only compulsory, harmful fare.
The blessed are told to eat and drink pleasantly for what they did; this supplies the good bodily state completed by the fruit and meat in 52:22.
A bitterly cold wind destroys the crop of people who wronged themselves; the parable turns cultivated food into loss, another specific passage from expected nourishment to ruined vegetation.
The garden owner is warned that its water may sink beyond recovery, identifying loss of drink as one route by which productive land ceases to provide.
The garden's fruit is encompassed and its trellises collapse, completing the reversal from abundant produce to a provision that can no longer be gathered.
Mary is told to shake the palm so fresh ripe dates fall to her; a fruit tree answers acute bodily vulnerability with accessible nourishment.
“Eat, drink, and be comforted” joins food, drink, and inward relief in one command, the fullest positive opposite to a meal that neither fattens nor removes lack.
